47/54★ Must-learnWays and Means Advances

In plain words

The central bank extends short-term credit facilities to the government to bridge temporary gaps between cash receipts and expenditure.

Why it exists

  • Government revenue collections arrive unevenly during the year, while ongoing welfare and administrative commitments must be disbursed smoothly.
  • It prevents the government from borrowing impulsively from open markets at high yields during brief cash-flow deficits.

How it works

  • The central bank and the government fix advance limits for each half of the fiscal year based on projected expenditure profiles.
  • When the government draws funds within the limit, interest is charged at the benchmark repo rate.
  • If the drawdown persists beyond agreed ceilings or durations, punitive overdraft interest applies above the standard repo rate.
  • Reaching high utilization triggers formal debt issuances in sovereign bond markets.

Fixed facts

  • WMA: introduced 1 Apr 1997 under Section 17(5) RBI Act (replaced ad-hoc treasury bills); 90 days; states' Special Drawing Facility 1% below repo

Traps

  • Ways and Means Advances are not permanent budget deficit financing; they must be cleared within ninety days.
  • The facility carries interest at the repo rate rather than zero cost, with higher punitive rates for extended overdrafts.

In the news

  • September 2026: RBI fixes H2 FY27 Ways and Means Advances limit at ₹50,000 crore

48/54★ Must-learnFloating Rate Bonds

In plain words

Sovereign debt securities whose interest coupons periodically reset based on prevailing benchmark Treasury bill yields plus a predetermined spread.

Why it exists

  • Fixed-rate bonds expose investors and the sovereign issuer to interest rate risk when market rates fluctuate over extended horizons.
  • Variable coupon structures offer protection against inflation and changing yield environments, expanding debt absorption capacity.

How it works

  • The sovereign issues debt securities with coupon payments linked directly to short-term money market auctions.
  • At each scheduled reset date, the coupon is recalculated from recent auction yields plus the fixed spread.
  • Interest is paid half-yearly to bondholders until final principal redemption at maturity.

Fixed facts

  • Linked to 182-day T-Bill yield: average weighted average yield of last 3 auctions + fixed spread 0.64 pp . Reset every 6 months; interest paid half-yearly.

How it changed

  • October 2026: RBI fixed FRB 2028 rate at 6.45% for 4 Oct 2026 – 3 Apr 2027 .

Traps

  • Floating rate bond coupons fluctuate with short-term market yields, unlike conventional fixed-rate sovereign securities.
  • The spread above the benchmark remains constant throughout the bond tenure even as the base yield fluctuates.

In the news

  • October 2026: FRB 2028 coupon

49/54★ Must-learnCentral Bank Digital Currency (Digital Rupee)

In plain words

Sovereign digital legal tender issued directly by the monetary authority representing a direct sovereign claim on the central bank balance sheet.

Why it exists

  • Physical currency management incurs high printing, transport, security, and distribution costs across nationwide networks.
  • A sovereign digital token combines the direct liability status of banknotes with digital settlement speed and programmable conditional execution.

How it works

  • The central bank issues digital tokens to licensed intermediary banks through wholesale and retail pilots.
  • Individuals and commercial enterprises store sovereign tokens in dedicated digital wallets without requiring commercial bank deposits.
  • Transactions settle immediately on distributed or centralised sovereign ledger infrastructure with optional programmability parameters.

Fixed facts

  • Wholesale CBDC launched 1 Nov 2022 (interbank)
  • Retail CBDC launched 1 Dec 2022 (public)

How it changed

  • September 2026: Users can schedule automatic e₹ transfers to a beneficiary’s CBDC wallet; tech partner Montran India
  • March 2026: Pilot in PDS (public distribution system): digital coupons through RBI credited as programmable e₹; redeemed at fair price shops; districts Ahmedabad, Anand, Valsad, Surat; to extend to Chandigarh, Puducherry, DNHDD; slogan "Har Dana, Har Rupiya, Har Adhikar"

Traps

  • A digital rupee is a direct liability of the central bank rather than a commercial bank deposit or private digital balance.
  • Wholesale tokens facilitate interbank settlements, whereas retail tokens serve general public transactions.

In the news

  • September 2026: Bank of India launches programmable Digital Rupee (e₹)
  • January–March 2026: CBDC-based digital food coupon pilot (Gujarat)

50/54★ Must-learnTrade Receivables Discounting System

In plain words

An institutional electronic auction platform enabling micro, small, and medium enterprises to auction trade receivables and obtain immediate financing.

Why it exists

  • Small suppliers frequently face severe cash-flow delays when large buyers defer invoice payments over extended durations.
  • Competitive bidding by multiple financiers against accepted invoices allows small enterprises to access low-cost working capital quickly.

How it works

  • The small enterprise supplier uploads accepted trade invoices onto the licensed platform.
  • The corporate or government buyer confirms and accepts the invoice details electronically.
  • Banks and financial institutions bid against the receivable, discounting the invoice and paying funds directly to the small enterprise supplier.

Fixed facts

  • TReDS Platform operator needs net worth of ₹25 crore; participants are sellers, buyers, financiers, insurers and NCGTC

How it changed

  • September 2026: Aim: timely working capital for Micro and Small Enterprises
  • September 2026: M1xchange: first TReDS platform to operationalise it; CGTMSE CEO Manish Sinha

Traps

  • The discounting is conducted on an electronic auction exchange without recourse to the small enterprise supplier.
  • Eligible sellers on the exchange are restricted to micro, small, and medium enterprises.

In the news

  • September 2026: TReDS receivables can now get CGTMSE guarantee cover

51/54★ Must-learnSelf-Regulatory Organisations in financial markets

In plain words

Non-governmental industry bodies recognised by statutory authorities to establish codes of conduct, monitor market integrity, and settle disputes.

Why it exists

  • Rapidly innovating financial sectors require specialized oversight that cannot be micromanaged directly by statutory regulators.
  • Industry-led peer supervision encourages high ethical standards, consumer protection, and faster resolution of market frictions.

How it works

  • Market participants form an independent non-profit entity representing the sector under approved statutory governance norms.
  • The statutory authority grants formal recognition after verifying governance safeguards, independence, and operational capabilities.
  • The entity monitors compliance, resolves consumer grievances, and serves as an institutional bridge between industry and regulators.

Fixed facts

  • SRO = non-government body authorised by a regulator to oversee a sector
  • Role: enforce standards, ethical conduct, market integrity, dispute resolution, transparency
  • FEDAI (Foreign Exchange Dealers' Association of India): set up 1958, association of Authorised Dealer banks, incorporated under Section 25 of Companies Act 1956

How it changed

  • September 2026: First SRO-FT: FACE (Fintech Association for Consumer Empowerment)

Traps

  • A self-regulatory organisation does not replace statutory regulation; it operates under powers delegated by the central authority.
  • Industry bodies must maintain full operational independence and representative coverage to secure official recognition.

In the news

  • September 2026: RBI recognises Unified Fintech Forum as SRO-FT
  • January–March 2026: RBI recognises FEDAI as an SRO

52/54★ Must-learnAccount Aggregator financial data ecosystem

In plain words

A regulated consent-based digital intermediary network that securely transfers customer financial information between institutions without storing data.

Why it exists

  • Consumers and small businesses faced severe friction obtaining and sharing physical financial records across dispersed financial institutions.
  • Standardised data flows with explicit consent enable frictionless credit appraisal, financial planning, and inclusive digital lending.

How it works

  • A financial user requests specific historical data with customer permission through an aggregator application.
  • The customer grants digital consent specifying data types, purpose, and validity periods.
  • The financial information provider encrypts and transmits the data directly to the user through the aggregator pipeline without intermediary decryption.

Fixed facts

  • AA = RBI-licensed entity moving financial data between institutions only with customer consent; it cannot read or store the data.
  • Key figures: 17 Account Aggregators; 176 FIPs.

How it changed

  • October 2026: 31 Dec 2026 Deadline: Account Aggregator network interoperability

Traps

  • Aggregators act strictly as encrypted data conduits; they are legally forbidden from storing, viewing, or monetising client data.
  • Data transfers require explicit granular consent from the customer rather than blanket institutional authorisations.

In the news

  • October 2026: Account Aggregator network must be interoperable by 31 December 2026

53/54★ Must-learnPrepaid Payment Instruments directions

In plain words

Payment instruments that facilitate purchase of goods and financial services against pre-stored monetary value maintained in cards or wallets.

Why it exists

  • Unregulated issuance of digital stored-value wallets could jeopardize user funds and compromise national payment security standards.
  • Comprehensive prudential norms establish net worth thresholds, loading limits, and customer verification safeguards.

How it works

  • Entities obtain statutory authorisation from the central payments authority after meeting net worth criteria.
  • Customers load funds into cards or digital wallets using bank accounts or approved payment methods.
  • The pre-stored balance is debited in real time as the customer makes merchant purchases or fund transfers.

Fixed facts

  • Banks (debit card issuers) can issue PPIs with prior intimation to DPSS; non-banks need RBI authorisation and ₹15 cr net worth by end of third financial year
  • General-purpose PPI: outstanding balance up to ₹2 lakh; cash loading ₹10,000 per month
  • Gift PPI up to ₹10,000; Transit PPI ₹3,000; wallets for foreign nationals/NRIs (passport + visa) for P2M payments

Traps

  • Non-bank issuers must meet strict net worth thresholds and regulatory approvals, whereas banks issue instruments under prior intimation.
  • General-purpose instruments permit merchant purchases subject to regulatory ceilings, unlike closed single-merchant vouchers.

In the news

  • April 2026: RBI draft Master Direction on Prepaid Payment Instruments 2026

54/54★ Must-learnUrban Co-operative Banks regulatory tiers

In plain words

A four-tier regulatory classification system governing capital adequacy, unsecured credit caps, housing loan tenures, and governance in urban co-operatives.

Why it exists

  • Co-operative banking institutions range from tiny single-branch societies to massive multi-state scheduled banks with thousands of depositors.
  • Graduated tier regulations ensure proportionate regulatory oversight while preventing governance concentration and unsecured exposure risks.

How it works

  • Institutions are classified into four distinct tiers based on total deposit size and operational spread.
  • Regulatory directions enforce exposure limits on unsecured lending and prescribe ceilings on residential mortgage maturities across tiers.
  • Statutory cooling-off rules prevent board members from serving indefinite uninterrupted tenures on the same institutional board.

Fixed facts

  • Unsecured loans and advances: aggregate ceiling 20% of total loans and advances (audited balance sheet of the preceding year)
  • Housing loans: Tier 1 and Tier 2 UCBs → tenure up to 20 years, including any moratorium; Tier 3 and Tier 4 → tenure and moratorium set by Board-approved policy

How it changed

  • April 2026: Amendment Directions issued 29 April 2026: Credit Facilities, Concentration Risk Management, Financial Statements (disclosures)
  • May 2026: Continuous tenure of 10 years → re-appointment on the same bank's board (election, co-option or otherwise) only after a cooling-off of 3 years
  • May 2026: RBI Governance Amendment Directions 2026 for UCBs and RCBs; immediate effect

Traps

  • Tier one and tier two urban co-operative banks face statutory housing loan tenure caps, whereas higher tiers set tenures under board policies.
  • Continuous tenure limits require mandatory cooling-off periods before re-appointment to the same institutional board.

In the news

  • May 2026: Co-operative bank directors: three-year cooling-off
  • April 2026: RBI: lending norms for urban co-operative banks (final)

Static Bank · Section 3GST, Taxation and Budget14 items · 9 ★ must-learn · 5 ☆ good to know

Memory tricks

GST is a single tax on supply of goods and services, replacing many older taxes; the Centre, States and the GST Council share it.

Direct taxes (income tax) are paid by the person taxed; indirect taxes (GST, customs) are collected through the price.

The Budget lists the Government's receipts and spending for the year; a deficit means spending is more than receipts.

Reading order: GST → direct and indirect tax → Income-tax Act → Budget → deficits and the FRBM Act.

3.1 GST journey

1/14★ Must-learnGST timeline

In plain words

GST took about two decades to arrive, from first talks in 2000 to launch in 2017; the timeline shows each step on the way.

YearEvent
2000Vajpayee government begins GST discussions; Asim Dasgupta-led Empowered Committee of state finance ministers
2006-07Budget speech (P Chidambaram) announces GST from 1 Apr 2010
2009Empowered Committee's First Discussion Paper on GST (Nov 2009); 13th Finance Commission Task Force on GST (chair Arbind Modi)
2011115th Constitution Amendment Bill (lapsed)
2013GSTN (Goods and Services Tax Network) set up as a Section 8 company
Dec 2014122nd Amendment Bill introduced (Arun Jaitley); Lok Sabha passed May 2015; Rajya Sabha Aug 2016
Sep 2016101st Amendment Act (assent 8 Sep) → GST Council constituted 12 Sep; first meeting 22–23 Sep 2016
1 Jul 2017GST launched at midnight session in Central Hall of Parliament (July 1 = GST Day)
Jul 2017J&K joins (8 Jul 2017) → "One Nation, One Tax, One Market"
2018E-way bill (1 Apr 2018)
3 Sep 202556th GST Council → two-slab structure, effective 22 Sep 2025 ("GST 2.0")
Exam angle

Which Amendment, which Article, which date?

Memory tricks

Idea 2000 → announced 2006 → Bill 2014 → Amendment 2016 → Launch 2017 → 2.0 in 2025. "Sixteen to Seventeen": Act 2016, launch 2017.

2/14★ Must-learnGST structure and Acts

In plain words

GST is one tax on goods and services that replaced many separate taxes; it is split into central, state and inter-state parts depending on where the sale happens.

TaxLevied onGoes to
CGST (Central GST)Intra-state supplyCentre
SGST (State GST)Intra-state supplyState
IGST (Integrated GST)Inter-state supply and importsCollected by Centre, apportioned to the destination state
UTGST (Union Territory GST)Intra-UT supply (UTs without legislature)UT
Compensation CessSin and luxury goodsCompensation Fund (from 22 Sep 2025 merged into the 40% rate, except pan masala, gutkha and tobacco products)
  • Dual GST → Centre and states both levy | destination-based | input tax credit (ITC) chain
  • Acts of 2017 → CGST, IGST, UTGST, GST (Compensation to States) Act (5 years of compensation; 14% annual growth over the 2015-16 base)
  • Constitutional hooks → 246A (power), 269A (inter-state levy), 279A (Council), 366(12A) (definition)
  • Outside GST at launch → crude oil, diesel, petrol, natural gas, aviation turbine fuel; alcohol for human consumption; electricity (not subsumed)
Memory tricks

"CSI-U": CGST, SGST, IGST, UTGST. IGST = Inter-state, Import. Intra = CGST + SGST together (equal split).

3.2 GST Council

3/14★ Must-learnGST Council (Art 279A)

In plain words

The GST Council is the joint forum where the Centre and States decide GST rates and rules together.

  • Inserted by 101st Amendment 2016; President constitutes it | joint forum of Centre and states | office in New Delhi
  • Chair → Union Finance Minister | members → Union MoS (Finance/Revenue) + state finance/taxation ministers (one among them elected Vice-Chair)
  • Secretary → Union Revenue Secretary (ex-officio) | CBIC Chairperson is a permanent invitee (no vote)
  • Voting → Centre 1/3 weight, all states together 2/3 | decision needs 3/4 of weighted votes of members present and voting
  • Recommends → taxes subsumed, exemptions, rates (including floor rates), model laws, IGST apportionment, special provisions for hill and north-east states, compensation
  • Supreme Court (2022, Mohit Minerals) → Council recommendations are persuasive, not binding
Memory tricks

1/3 + 2/3 = 100% of weight; 3/4 needed. Neither side can pass a decision alone (33% and 67% are both below 75%). The Centre alone can block, since its 33% is above the 25% blocking minority. Remember "1/3, 2/3, 3/4".

Why it exists

  • Multiple cascading state and central indirect taxes created internal economic barriers and excessive compliance burdens.
  • A destination-based shared tax structure standardises nationwide tariffs and eliminates tax cascading across interstate value chains.

How it works

  • A joint constitutional body comprising federal and state finance ministers deliberates on tax slabs, exemptions, and compliance rules.
  • Transactions attract split central and state levies or an integrated levy on interstate commerce with seamless input credit transfers.
  • Electronic declarations and automated invoice tracking verify supply chain transactions and credit settlement across jurisdictions.

More fixed facts

  • GST Council: created by Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016; chaired by Union Finance Minister
  • GST Council voting? Show answer Centre 1/3, States 2/3; decisions need 3/4 of weighted votes.

How it changed

  • October 2026: Arrest powers withdrawn: omit Section 69, CGST Act 2017. Prosecution threshold ₹1 cr → ₹5 cr; Section 132 narrowed (clause c only for fake-ITC without goods/services/invoice). Max general penalty (Section 125) ₹25,000 → ₹10,000.

Traps

  • Council decisions require a three-fourths weighted majority giving neither Centre nor States unilateral veto power alone.
  • Taxation of petroleum crude and select fuels remains deferred until recommended by the federal council.

In the news

  • Nov 2026: GST collections, October 2026: ₹2.31 lakh crore gross
  • Oct 2026: IGST on gold, silver, platinum imports
  • Oct 2026: 57th GST Council meeting: rate rationalisation decisions
  • Sep 2026: 56th GST Council meeting decisions
  • Jan Mar 2026: GST collections FY26 reach record high

4/14★ Must-learnGST 2.0: slab overhaul of 2025

In plain words

In 2025 the GST rate structure was simplified into fewer slabs; this card gives the date and the new rates.

  • 56th Council → 3 Sep 2025 (chair: Nirmala Sitharaman) → unanimous | effective 22 Sep 2025 (tobacco from 1 Feb 2026: 40% GST on cigarettes, pan masala and tobacco, 18% on bidis; the compensation cess replaced by excise and a health and national security cess)
  • Four slabs 5 / 12 / 18 / 28 → two slabs 5% (merit) and 18% (standard), plus special 40% (demerit/luxury)
BeforeAfterExamples
28%18%ACs, TVs, dishwashers, small cars, cement
12% / 18%5%Toothpaste, umbrellas, sewing machines, bicycles, FMCG sachets
18%NilIndividual life and health insurance premiums
28%40%Luxury cars and SUVs, tobacco products, pan masala
Cess items40% (cess merged)Aerated drinks, casinos, online gaming, race clubs
  • 12% and 28% slabs abolished | estimated revenue loss over ₹47,000 crore
Memory tricks

"5-18-40": merit, standard, sin. Four slabs became two plus one special.

5/14☆ Good to knowRegistration, composition and GSTN

  • Registration threshold → ₹40 lakh (goods), ₹20 lakh (services); lower for special category states
  • Composition scheme → turnover up to ₹1.5 crore (goods)
  • GSTN → IT backbone; became 100% government-owned in 2019
  • CBIC (Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs) administers GST and customs; renamed from CBEC in 2017
Remember

These thresholds changed over the years; keep as indicative until verified.

3.3 Taxation basics

6/14★ Must-learnDirect vs indirect taxes

In plain words

Direct taxes are paid by the person on whom they are levied; indirect taxes are collected from a buyer through the price of what is bought.

DirectIndirect
BurdenCannot be shiftedShifted to consumer
ExamplesIncome tax, corporate tax, capital gains tax, STT (Securities Transaction Tax, 2004)GST, customs duty, central excise (on petroleum and a few items)
BodyCBDT (Central Board of Direct Taxes)CBIC
NatureProgressive (rate rises with income)Regressive in effect (same rate for all)
  • Income tax first introduced in India in 1860 by James Wilson | Income Tax Day → 24 July
  • Wealth tax abolished from Budget 2015-16 (replaced by a surcharge on the super-rich)
  • Cess and surcharge are not shared with states (outside the divisible pool)
Memory tricks

Direct = DIrect hit on the taxpayer (CBDT). Indirect = INcluded in price (CBIC).

7/14★ Must-learnIncome-tax Act, 2025

In plain words

India has replaced its 1961 income-tax law with a new Act from 1 April 2026; this card gives the dates and key facts.

  • Replaced the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Act 43 of 1961) from 1 Apr 2026
  • Act 30 of 2025 | Presidential assent 21 Aug 2025 | first Income-tax Bill introduced 13 Feb 2025, withdrawn 8 Aug 2025, revised Bill passed
  • Sections 819 → 536 | Chapters 47 → 23 | Schedules → 16
  • "Previous Year" and "Assessment Year" replaced by one "Tax Year" (Section 3) → income of 2026-27 = Tax Year 2026-27
  • Policy-neutral: no new taxes, no change in rates, slabs or regimes
  • Transition → FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27) returns still under the 1961 Act
  • TDS compressed into 3 sections (392 to 394)
Exam angle

When did the new Act come into force and what replaced the assessment-year concept?

Memory tricks

819 → 536 (about a third cut) | 47 → 23 chapters | 1961 → 2025, in force 2026. "Tax Year" = one year replaces two (previous and assessment).

8/14☆ Good to knowCapital gains: LTCG and STCG

AssetLong-term if heldLTCG rateShort-term
Listed shares, equity mutual funds, business trust unitsMore than 12 months12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh a year20% (STCG on listed equity)
Property, gold, unlisted shares, other assetsMore than 24 months12.5%, no indexationSlab rates
Debt mutual funds (since Apr 2023)–Slab rates, any holding periodSlab rates
  • Budget July 2024: LTCG on listed equity 10% → 12.5%; exemption ₹1 lakh → ₹1.25 lakh; STCG 15% → 20%; indexation removed from 23 Jul 2024
  • Land or building bought before 23 Jul 2024: resident individual / HUF may choose 12.5% without indexation or 20% with indexation
  • Old Act sections: 111A (STCG on listed equity), 112A (LTCG on listed equity); the Income-tax Act 2025 (in force 1 Apr 2026) renumbers sections
  • STT (Securities Transaction Tax) is separate from capital gains tax
Remember

Equity: 12 months, 12.5%, ₹1.25 lakh exempt. Short-term: 20%.

9/14☆ Good to knowCustoms duty and import levies

DutyLegal basisWhat it does
BCD (Basic Customs Duty)Sec 12, Customs Act 1962Main import duty on assessable value (Sec 14)
SWS (Social Welfare Surcharge)Sec 110, Finance Act 2018Surcharge on top of BCD
IGST on importsSec 5, IGST Act 2017 with Sec 3(7), Customs Tariff ActReplaces the old additional duties for GST goods
CVD (Countervailing Duty)Sec 9, Customs Tariff Act 1975Offsets a foreign subsidy

  • CBIC (Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs) administers customs and GST
  • DGTR (Directorate General of Trade Remedies) recommends anti-dumping and safeguard duties; the Finance Ministry notifies them
Memory tricks

Section numbers: 8B – 9 – 9A = Safeguard (surge), CVD (subsidy), ADD (dumping).

3.4 Budget basics

10/14★ Must-learnBudget in the Constitution

In plain words

The Constitution sets out how the Budget is presented and passed; each Article covers one step.

ArtSubject
112Annual Financial Statement (Budget)
113Procedure in Parliament (demands for grants)
114Appropriation Bill
115Supplementary, additional, excess grants
116Vote on account, vote of credit, exceptional grants
117Financial Bills
265No tax without law
266Consolidated Fund (1) and Public Account (2)
267Contingency Fund (President's advance)
  • Budget presented on 1 Feb (from 2017; earlier last working day of February) | Rail Budget merged with Union Budget from 2017-18
  • Plan / non-plan classification abolished 2017-18 → now revenue / capital
  • Two Bills follow the Budget → Appropriation Bill authorises withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund; Finance Bill carries the tax proposals
Memory tricks

112-113-114-115-116-117 reads "Budget, Demand, Appropriation, Supplementary, Vote on account, Financial Bills". 266 = fundS (Consolidated + Public), 267 = emergency fund.

Why it exists

  • Democratic accountability requires legislative authorization before the executive can levy taxes or withdraw public revenues.
  • A comprehensive pre-budget survey provides an analytical evaluation of macroeconomic fundamentals to inform parliamentary scrutiny.

How it works

  • The finance ministry collects spending estimates from administrative departments and coordinates economic forecasting.
  • The chief economic adviser prepares an economic report evaluating macroeconomic performance across domestic sectors.
  • The finance minister presents the annual financial statement in parliament for general debate, department scrutiny, and vote on taxes.

More fixed facts

  • First Economic Survey 1950-51; prepared by the Economic Division, Department of Economic Affairs (Ministry of Finance) under the Chief Economic Adviser (V. Anantha Nageswaran since 28 Jan 2022)
  • Tabled in Parliament by the Finance Minister one day before the Union Budget
  • Separated from the Budget speech in 1964; since 2022-23 one consolidated volume plus a Statistical Appendix (earlier two volumes)

How it changed

  • January 2026: Tabled by FM Nirmala Sitharaman in Lok Sabha; prepared under CEA V. Anantha Nageswaran
  • January 2026: Real GDP growth projection FY27: 6.8–7.2%

Traps

  • The Economic Survey is presented by convention and is not mandated by the Constitution.
  • Appropriation and finance bills follow distinct parliamentary passage and voting procedures.

In the news

  • Jan Mar 2026: Economic Survey 2025-26 tabled in Parliament
  • Jan Mar 2026: Union Budget 2026-27 presented

11/14★ Must-learnReceipts, expenditure and deficits

In plain words

Receipts are money the Government gets, expenditure is what it spends, and a deficit measures how much it falls short; the formulas show how each deficit is calculated.

ItemFormula / meaning
Revenue receiptsTax revenue + non-tax revenue (no liability created, no asset reduced)
Capital receiptsBorrowings, recovery of loans, disinvestment (create liability or reduce asset)
Revenue deficitRevenue expenditure − Revenue receipts
Effective revenue deficitRevenue deficit − grants for creation of capital assets
Fiscal deficitTotal expenditure − (Revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts) = borrowing need
Primary deficitFiscal deficit − Interest payments
Budgetary deficitOld measure; abolished from 1997-98
Memory tricks

"R → F → P": Revenue deficit, Fiscal deficit, Primary deficit. Primary = Fiscal minus interest. Fiscal deficit = how much the government must borrow.

Why it exists

  • Public investment and welfare expenditures frequently exceed current tax revenues, requiring prudential sovereign debt financing.
  • A predictable and transparent issuance calendar prevents market disruption and ensures orderly sovereign yield curve formation.

How it works

  • The union government determines its net borrowing requirement during the annual budget presentation.
  • The central bank issues dated securities and treasury bills through regular competitive electronic auctions.
  • Institutional investors purchase bonds to fund infrastructure outlays while the sovereign manages repayment tenors.

More fixed facts

  • Gross market borrowing BE ₹17.20 lakh crore → ₹16.09 lakh crore after G-Sec switches
  • FY27 fiscal deficit target 4.3% of GDP

How it changed

  • September 2026: Exact total ₹15,99,506 cr; H2 plan ₹7,86,000 cr (incl. ₹15,000 cr Sovereign Green Bonds) via 23 weekly auctions; tenors 3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 30, 40, 50 yrs; greenshoe ₹2,000 cr; H2 WMA limit ₹50,000 cr
  • March 2026: Gross market borrowing BE ₹17.20 lakh crore → ₹16.09 lakh crore after G-Sec switches

Traps

  • The borrowing programme is financed through dated securities and treasury bills rather than direct central bank deficit financing.
  • Fiscal deficit figures include net market borrowing alongside other internal liabilities.

In the news

  • Sep 2026: Centre releases H2 FY27 borrowing calendar
  • Mar 2026: Centre releases H1 FY27 borrowing calendar
  • Jan Mar 2026: Union Budget 2026-27: fiscal deficit roadmap

12/14☆ Good to knowBudget passage and cut motions

  • Stages → presentation → general discussion → scrutiny by departmentally related standing committees → voting on demands for grants (Lok Sabha only; guillotine closes undiscussed demands) → Appropriation Bill → Finance Bill
  • Cut motions → policy cut (₹1 symbolic; disapproves policy), economy cut (specified amount), token cut (₹100; grievance)
  • Rajya Sabha only discusses; does not vote on demands for grants
  • Vote on account → temporary spending cover before the Budget passes (Art 116) | interim budget in election years

13/14★ Must-learnFRBM Act and the N K Singh Committee

In plain words

The FRBM Act sets limits on the Government's borrowing and deficits; the N K Singh Committee reviewed it and suggested new targets.

  • FRBM Act 2003 (Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management) | rules 2004 | fiscal deficit target 3% of GDP
  • N K Singh Committee → set up May 2016, report Jan 2017 (five members)
  • Recommendations → debt-to-GDP 60% (Centre 40% + states 20%) by 2023 | fiscal deficit 3% for 2017-20, then 2.5% by 2022-23 | escape clause up to 0.5% of GDP | three-member independent Fiscal Council | replace FRBM with a Debt and Fiscal Responsibility Act
  • Government accepted the debt anchor and escape clause in part; the Fiscal Council was not set up as recommended
Memory tricks

"60 = 40 + 20", "3 → 2.5", "0.5 escape".

14/14☆ Good to knowEconomic Survey

  • First Economic Survey 1950-51; prepared by the Economic Division, Department of Economic Affairs (Ministry of Finance) under the Chief Economic Adviser (V. Anantha Nageswaran since 28 Jan 2022)
  • Tabled in Parliament by the Finance Minister one day before the Union Budget
  • No constitutional or statutory mandate: a convention
  • Separated from the Budget speech in 1964; since 2022-23 one consolidated volume plus a Statistical Appendix (earlier two volumes)
Remember

Survey = convention, not law. Budget = Art 112 (Annual Financial Statement).

Static Bank · Section 4Financial Regulators and Institutions23 items · 14 ★ must-learn · 9 ☆ good to know

Memory tricks

A regulator is a body with legal power to set rules for one part of finance and to supervise it.

RBI: banks and payments. SEBI: shares and mutual funds. IRDAI: insurance. PFRDA: pensions. Each card gives the set-up date, HQ and law.

All India Financial Institutions (NABARD, EXIM, SIDBI and similar) are not regulators but lenders for one sector each.

4.1 Who regulates whom

1/23★ Must-learnRegulator map

In plain words

Each segment of the financial system has its own regulator; this map shows which regulator watches which part.

RegulatorRegulates
RBIBanks, NBFCs, housing finance companies (since 2019), payment systems, credit bureaus, cooperative banks (with NABARD supervising RRBs and rural cooperatives), forex
SEBIStock exchanges, brokers, mutual funds, depositories, AIFs, credit rating agencies, commodity derivatives (FMC merged into SEBI in 2015)
IRDAIInsurers, reinsurers, insurance intermediaries
PFRDANPS, pension funds, Atal Pension Yojana
IFSCAFinancial services in IFSC (GIFT City)
IBBIInsolvency professionals and agencies under IBC 2016

Memory tricks

"B-M-I-P": Banks → RBI, Markets → SEBI, Insurance → IRDAI, Pensions → PFRDA.

2/23☆ Good to knowHow regulator heads are chosen (FSRASC)

  • FSRASC (Financial Sector Regulatory Appointments Search Committee) → set up from the FSLRC (Justice B N Srikrishna Commission) recommendation; recommends heads and members of SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, and RBI Governor and Deputy Governors
  • Composition → Cabinet Secretary (chair); Additional Principal Secretary to PM; Secretary DEA or DFS; chair of the concerned regulator; three outside experts
  • Final approval → Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC)
  • For PSB and financial institution heads → FSIB (Financial Services Institutions Bureau)
Remember

Search committee recommends; ACC (chaired by PM) approves.

4.2 SEBI

3/23★ Must-learnSEBI at a glance

In plain words

SEBI regulates the securities market, meaning shares, bonds and mutual funds; it began in 1988 and got legal powers in 1992.

  • Set up 12 Apr 1988 (non-statutory, under Finance Ministry) → statutory under the SEBI Act 1992 (statutory powers from 30 Jan 1992, after the Harshad Mehta scam) | HQ Mumbai (BKC)
  • Replaced the Controller of Capital Issues (Capital Issues (Control) Act 1947): merit-based control → disclosure-based regulation
  • Board (s.4) → 9 members = Chairperson + 2 Finance Ministry officials + 1 RBI nominee + 5 other members (at least 3 whole-time)
  • Functions → s.11 | appeals → SAT (Securities Appellate Tribunal, set up 1997; working from 1 Nov 1997) | then Supreme Court
  • First woman Chairperson → Madhabi Puri Buch (2022 to Feb 2025, also first from private sector)
  • Current Chairperson → Tuhin Kanta Pandey, 11th Chairperson, took charge 1 Mar 2025 for 3 years (appointed by ACC on 27 Feb 2025)
  • Chairperson's term → up to 5 years or age 65 as appointed
Exam angle

Which Act gave SEBI statutory powers? Which body did it replace?

Memory tricks

88 born, 92 sworn: "Born 88, Statutory 92".

4/23★ Must-learnSecurities Markets Code, 2025 (pending Bill)

In plain words

This is a proposed Code to bring securities-market laws together; it is still a Bill, so it is not yet law.

  • Introduced in Lok Sabha on 18 Dec 2025 (Bill No. 200 of 2025) → referred to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance (report presented 23 Jul 2026)
  • Would repeal and replace → SCRA 1956, SEBI Act 1992 and Depositories Act 1996
  • Key proposals → SEBI Board enlarged from 9 to up to 15; separation of investigation and adjudication; mandatory registration of MIIs (Market Infrastructure Institutions: exchanges, depositories, clearing corporations); definition of market abuse; regulatory sandbox; conflict-of-interest disclosure by board members
  • Budget 2021 had announced the plan to consolidate the three Acts
Remember

Status: Bill, not yet an Act as of the last check (Oct 2026). Update this entry if it becomes law.

Memory tricks

Three old Acts → One Code: 1956 + 1992 + 1996 → 2025.

4.3 IRDAI and insurance

6/23★ Must-learnIRDAI at a glance

In plain words

IRDAI regulates the insurance sector; this card gives how it began, its law and its HQ.

  • Recommended by the Malhotra Committee (R N Malhotra, 1993) → IRDA Act 1999 → IRDAI statutory body formed in 2000 | HQ Hyderabad
  • Insurance Act 1938 | LIC (life insurance nationalised 1956; LIC Act 1956, formed 1 Sep 1956) | GIC and four subsidiaries (1972-73)
  • Current Chairman → Ajay Seth (former DEA Secretary), took charge 1 Sep 2025 for 3 years or age 65; succeeded Debasish Panda

"38, 56, 72, 99": Insurance Act, LIC nationalisation, general insurance nationalisation, IRDA Act.

7/23★ Must-learnSabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025

In plain words

This Act amends three insurance laws and raises the limit on foreign ownership of insurers to 100%.

  • Introduced in Lok Sabha 16 Dec 2025 → passed → now an Act
  • Amends three laws → Insurance Act 1938, LIC Act 1956, IRDA Act 1999
  • FDI 74% → 100% | conditions via the Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Amendment Rules, notified 30 Dec 2025
  • Penalty cap for non-compliance → ₹1 crore → ₹10 crore
  • Notified 21 Dec 2025; in force 5 Feb 2026 | IRDAI approval needed to transfer shares: threshold 1% → 5% | foreign reinsurer's net owned fund ₹5,000 crore → ₹1,000 crore | one-time registration of intermediaries
  • IRDAI powers expanded → order recovery of wrongful gains, supersede an insurer's board and appoint an administrator, inspect intermediaries
  • Creates a Policyholders' Education and Protection Fund | Insurance laws aligned with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023
  • Vision tag → "Insurance for All by 2047"
Exam angle

Which three Acts does it amend, and what is the new FDI limit?

8/23★ Must-learnIRDAI: Ind AS, D-SIIs and health insurance rules

In plain words

IRDAI has issued new accounting and health-insurance rules; the table gives the effective dates and the key points.

ItemKey facts
Ind AS for insurersFrom 1 Apr 2026; IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) (Amendment) Regulations 2026; applies to Life, General, Stand-Alone Health insurers and reinsurers (earlier IGAAP); parallel reporting for 2 years; one-year forbearance if an insurer cannot comply; Ind AS is converged with IFRS and implemented by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs
D-SIIs (Domestic Systemically Important Insurers)FY2025-26: LIC, GIC Re, New India Assurance retain status (too big to fail by size, importance and interconnectedness)
Health insurance rulesMoratorium 8 → 5 years (60 months); 30-day free look; grace period 15 days (monthly) or 30 days (other modes); pro-rata refund on mid-term cancellation
GSTIndividual life and health policies (incl. family floater) and reinsurance exempt from 22 Sep 2025 (was 18%)

Remember

D-SIIs = LIC + GIC Re (state-owned reinsurer) + New India. D-SIBs = SBI, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank.

Exam angle

Name the three D-SIIs. Since when must insurers follow Ind AS?

Why it exists

  • Insurance contracts involve deferred promises requiring strict financial solvency standards to guarantee claim settlement capabilities.
  • Statutory product norms, underwriting disclosures, and capital reserve rules protect policyholders from arbitrary claim repudiation.

How it works

  • Insurers and intermediaries obtain operating licences and maintain statutory solvency margins determined by actuarial calculations.
  • Underwriters evaluate risks, collect policyholder premiums, and maintain dedicated technical reserves in approved asset classes.
  • Claims are adjudicated under mandatory ombudsman and consumer protection regulations enforcing prompt fair settlement.

More fixed facts

  • Health rules: moratorium 8 → 5 years (60 months) (2024); 30-day free look; grace period 15 days (monthly) or 30 days (other modes); pro-rata refund on mid-term cancellation
  • IRDAI D-SIIs for FY 2025-26: LIC, New India Assurance and GIC Re (unchanged)

How it changed

  • May 2026: Finance Ministry notification: 100% FDI in insurance under automatic route; insurance intermediaries 100%
  • April 2026: IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) (Amendment) Regulations 2026, approved at its 135th meeting

Traps

  • Systemically important domestic insurers maintain additional capital standards due to distress contagion risks.
  • Policyholder grievance redressal follows mandatory response timelines enforced across insurance companies.

In the news

  • Nov 2026: IRDAI master circular: share-transfer fee cut 80% (2 Nov)
  • Oct 2026: IRDAI proposes overhaul of insurance distribution framework
  • Sep 2026: BMIP

4.4 PFRDA

9/23★ Must-learnPFRDA and pensions

In plain words

PFRDA regulates pensions, including the National Pension System, which was started for government employees and then opened to all.

  • Interim authority set up 2003 by government resolution → statutory under PFRDA Act 2013 (in force Feb 2014) | HQ New Delhi
  • NPS (National Pension System) → central government employees from 2004; all citizens from 2009
  • APY (Atal Pension Yojana) → 2015 (unorganised sector)
  • NPS Vatsalya → announced in Budget 2024-25, launched 18 Sep 2024; for minors (under 18, incl. NRI/OCI) through a guardian; minimum ₹250 a year, no maximum; partial withdrawal after 3 years up to 25% of own contribution; at 18 fresh KYC and choice (by 21) to continue, move to NPS Tier I or exit (80% lump sum, 20% annuity; full withdrawal if corpus up to ₹8 lakh)
  • UPS (Unified Pension Scheme) → implemented 1 Apr 2025
  • Current Chairperson → Sivasubramanian Ramann, took charge 20 Jun 2025 for 5 years or age 65; earlier CMD of SIDBI (2021-24), Deputy CAG; succeeded Deepak Mohanty
Memory tricks

PFRDA: "03 interim, 13 Act". NPS 04 for government, 09 for all.

Why it exists

  • Demographic ageing and rising fiscal pension liabilities necessitated a transition from unfunded defined benefits to funded defined contributions.
  • Professional asset management under statutory oversight provides transparent wealth accumulation for old-age financial security.

How it works

  • Subscribers enroll through points of presence and receive a unique permanent retirement account number.
  • Contributions are allocated across regulated pension fund managers investing in equity, government debt, and corporate bonds.
  • Upon reaching retirement age, a portion of the accumulated corpus is converted into regular annuity payouts.

More fixed facts

  • PFRDA: PoP onboarding charge ₹200 per new subscriber (₹100 if fully digital); annual 0.20% of AUM; NPS minimum ₹250 first contribution, ₹10 later

How it changed

  • September 2026: Voluntary contributory pension scheme for medical expenses; pilot (Proof of Concept) in PFRDA's Regulatory Sandbox
  • January 2026: PFRDA panel on assured payouts under NPS: chair Dr M. S. Sahoo (ex-IBBI chair), 15 members

Traps

  • Retirement contributions accumulate in defined individual accounts rather than pooled defined benefit commitments.
  • Subscribers select asset allocation patterns across equity, corporate bonds, and government debt securities.

In the news

  • Oct 2026: BoB enters pension fund business
  • Oct 2026: NPS Tatkal
  • Oct 2026: NPS Central platform for subscribers
  • Sep 2026: PFRDA reclassifies NPS Multiple Scheme Framework by equity share

15/23☆ Good to knowFIU-IND and the anti-money-laundering framework

  • FIU-IND (Financial Intelligence Unit–India): set up 2004; central agency to receive, analyse and share suspicious-transaction information
  • Works under PMLA 2002 (Prevention of Money Laundering Act); the Enforcement Directorate investigates and prosecutes
  • Enforces AML/CFT (anti-money-laundering / countering financing of terrorism) norms, including for virtual digital asset (VDA) providers

Why it exists

  • Illicit financial transactions and tax evasion networks undermine economic stability and fund criminal enterprises.
  • A dedicated intelligence processing agency detects illicit financial patterns and empowers investigative agencies with actionable intelligence.

How it works

  • Reporting entities including banks, intermediaries, and digital asset exchanges file statutory cash and suspicious transaction reports.
  • The intelligence unit analyses financial flows using cross-institutional databases and pattern recognition methodologies.
  • Actionable intelligence dossiers are disseminated to law enforcement and international intelligence counterparts for enforcement.

More fixed facts

  • FIU-IND Nov 2004 — Not statutory; reports to the Economic Intelligence Council headed by the Finance Minister; works under the PMLA, 2002
  • Reports to the Economic Intelligence Council (headed by Finance Minister); under Department of Revenue

How it changed

  • September 2026: Reports to the Economic Intelligence Council (headed by Finance Minister); under Department of Revenue

Traps

  • The intelligence unit acts as an analytical coordinating agency rather than conducting physical policing or arrests.
  • Obligated entities must transmit transaction alerts automatically based on objective monetary and risk thresholds.

In the news

  • Oct 2026: FIU-IND issues compliance notices to offshore crypto exchanges
  • May 2026: FIU-IND releases updated AML/CFT guidelines for reporting entities

  • Amended by the SCRR Amendment Rules 2026 (notified 13 Mar 2026): 25% MPS benchmark unchanged; big issuers get longer timelines

Why it exists

  • Foreign capital inflows deepen market liquidity but create risks of sudden capital flights during international crises.
  • Categorized registration and aggregate macro-prudential ceilings allow foreign capital participation while preserving domestic financial stability.

How it works

  • Overseas entities register through designated depository participants under regulatory categories matching their institutional structure.
  • Investors purchase listed equities, corporate bonds, and sovereign securities within established broad market ceilings.
  • Custodians monitor overall foreign investment caps and verify periodic customer identity compliance.

More fixed facts

  • SWAGAT-FI (Single Window Automatic and Generalized Access for Trusted Foreign Investors): unified registration for FPIs and FVCIs from 1 Jun 2026
  • FPIs may trade non-agricultural index derivatives and non-cash-settled non-agri commodity derivatives

How it changed

  • October 2026: KYC review periodicity: 1 year → 2 years; 3 years → 8 years (Category I FPIs and regulated Category II FPIs from non-high-risk jurisdictions get 8 years)
  • June 2026: SWAGAT-FI (Single Window Automatic and Generalized Access for Trusted Foreign Investors): unified registration for FPIs and FVCIs from 1 Jun 2026

Traps

  • Foreign investors must register under designated categories rather than operating without intermediary supervision.
  • Review periods vary depending on regulatory category and jurisdiction risk classification.

In the news

  • Oct 2026: SEBI eases KYC review periodicity for foreign portfolio investors
  • May 2026: SEBI: closing auction session (CAS) and FPI reforms
  • Jan Mar 2026: RBI: VRR folded into General Route

19/23★ Must-learnReal Estate and Infrastructure Investment Trusts

In plain words

Pooled investment trusts that own income-generating real estate or infrastructure assets and issue tradeable units to investors.

Why it exists

  • Direct acquisition of commercial real estate or infrastructure projects requires enormous capital beyond individual retail reach.
  • Trust structures aggregate distributed savings into professional grade operating assets while providing regular cash distributions.

How it works

  • A corporate sponsor transfers operational commercial property or infrastructure assets into an investment trust.
  • The trust raises capital by issuing units traded freely on stock exchanges to institutional and retail unitholders.
  • Operational earnings from property rentals or infrastructure user tolls are passed through to unitholders as periodic dividends.

Fixed facts

  • DR = foreign-currency instrument issued abroad against Indian securities held with a domestic custodian → lets overseas investors trade Indian units
  • Permitted exchanges: India INX and NSE IX (both IFSC, GIFT City)
  • DRs held only by non-residents
  • Units behind DRs cannot be priced below the price offered to Indian investors for a similar offering
  • Disclosures made on the international exchange → also filed with Indian exchanges within 24 hours; manager appoints a merchant banker
  • Privately placed InvITs: fresh DRs subscribed only by FIIs and corporate bodies

How it changed

  • November 2026: Fresh DR issue → approval of at least 75% of votes cast by unitholders; not needed for a simultaneous initial offer in India + DR listing abroad
  • April 2026: InvITs with net borrowings above 49% of asset value: fresh borrowings allowed for capex to enhance asset performance or capacity, major maintenance of road projects, and refinancing of principal only (regulations amended 17 April 2026)

Traps

  • Depository receipts backed by units can only be held by non-resident investors.
  • The pricing of underlying units cannot fall below the valuation offered to domestic Indian unitholders.

In the news

  • Nov 2026: SEBI permits depository receipts (DRs) for REITs and InvITs
  • Apr 2026: SEBI amends InvIT borrowing and SPV rules
  • Jan Mar 2026: RIIT (NHAI InvIT) listed on BSE

20/23★ Must-learnEquity and Commodity Derivatives risk framework

In plain words

A market risk containment framework comprising standardised risk indicators, auction sessions, position limits, and progressive penalty slabs.

Why it exists

  • Excessive speculative leverage and concentrated positions threaten market stability and retail investor capital safety.
  • Structured closing mechanisms and standardised disclosure meters ensure transparent risk assessment and orderly contract settlement.

How it works

  • The regulator defines objective categorisation criteria and prudential position caps for participating market entities.
  • Exchanges enforce price bands and designated auction intervals during market closing to prevent artificial price manipulation.
  • Surveillance systems compute daily position breaches and impose statutory penalties credited to investor protection funds.

Fixed facts

  • CAS in equity cash market: 20 minutes, 3:15–3:35 pm; starts with stocks having derivatives; price band ±3% of reference price; implemented from 3 Aug 2026; revised pre-open auction from 7 Sep 2026
  • Penalty per day: violation over 2% of limit → 2% of (excess × closing price) or ₹2,00,000, whichever lower; up to 2% → ₹10,000 cap; proceeds go to exchange Investor Protection Fund; >3 instances in a month → one-day square-off mode / double penalty
  • Client-level limits for agri commodities doubled: Broad 2%, Narrow 1%, Sensitive 0.5% of deliverable supply

How it changed

  • August 2026: CAS in equity cash market: 20 minutes, 3:15–3:35 pm; starts with stocks having derivatives; price band ±3% of reference price; implemented from 3 Aug 2026; revised pre-open auction from 7 Sep 2026
  • September 2026: Penalty per day: violation over 2% of limit → 2% of (excess × closing price) or ₹2,00,000, whichever lower; up to 2% → ₹10,000 cap; proceeds go to exchange Investor Protection Fund; >3 instances in a month → one-day square-off mode / double penalty

Traps

  • Closing auction sessions apply to designated cash equity scrips with active derivative contracts.
  • Position limit violation penalties are subject to progressive daily caps and enforcement measures.

In the news

  • Oct 2026: Credit Risk-o-Meter (colour-coded) mandatory
  • Oct 2026: CAS revised
  • Sep 2026: SEBI revises commodity derivatives position limits and penalties
  • May 2026: SEBI: closing auction session (CAS) and FPI reforms
  • Jan Mar 2026: SEBI circular: Credit Risk-o-Meter for mutual funds

21/23★ Must-learnSocial Stock Exchange segment

In plain words

A specialized stock exchange platform allowing registered non-profit and social enterprises to raise capital for public welfare activities.

Why it exists

  • Non-profit social organisations frequently struggle to secure sustained funding through conventional charity channels or bank lending.
  • An exchange-traded transparent mechanism connects social impact organisations with retail and institutional philanthropic funders.

How it works

  • Eligible social welfare organisations register on the exchange segment after satisfying governance criteria.
  • Entities issue specialised social financing instruments without commercial dividend or repayment obligations to raise contributions.
  • Annual impact reporting verifies social outcomes achieved with the raised philanthropic funds.

Fixed facts

  • Social Impact Fund Minimum investment by individuals cut from ₹2 lakh to ₹1,000
  • MCA: CSR can now go to Zero Coupon Zero Principal instruments on the Social Stock Exchange (new item xiii, Schedule VII, Companies Act 2013)

How it changed

  • October 2026: Social Impact Fund Minimum investment by individuals cut from ₹2 lakh to ₹1,000
  • January 2026: MCA: CSR can now go to Zero Coupon Zero Principal instruments on the Social Stock Exchange (new item xiii, Schedule VII, Companies Act 2013)

Traps

  • Instruments on this exchange segment carry zero interest coupons and return no principal at maturity.
  • Corporate CSR allocations can be deployed into eligible registered social impact issues.

In the news

  • Oct 2026: SEBI cuts minimum investment in Social Impact Funds to ₹1,000
  • Jan Mar 2026: Social Stock Exchange: NABARD subscribes to first ZCZP issue
  • Jan Mar 2026: MCA: CSR contributions eligible for Social Stock Exchange ZCZP instruments

22/23★ Must-learnPortfolio Management Services regulations

In plain words

A discretionary and non-discretionary investment framework where licensed professionals manage customized portfolios for high net worth clients.

Why it exists

  • Sophisticated high net worth investors require tailored investment strategies beyond standard retail pooled fund offerings.
  • Statutory manager qualification rules and minimum client investment thresholds ensure investor protection and fiduciary accountability.

How it works

  • A licensed manager enters into a formal fiduciary agreement with an eligible client possessing the statutory minimum corpus.
  • The manager invests client funds directly in approved securities, primary debt, or specialised funds matching the agreed risk profile.
  • Portfolio holdings remain directly owned in the client individual demat account and receive regular statutory valuation reports.

Fixed facts

  • SEBI (Portfolio Managers) Regulations, 2026 replace the 2020 rules; effective 1 Apr 2027.
  • Managers may invest in IPOs, debt primary issues, listed securities, money market instruments, mutual funds; also foreign securities, unlisted securities, exchange-traded derivatives.

How it changed

  • October 2026: SEBI (Portfolio Managers) Regulations, 2026 replace the 2020 rules; effective 1 Apr 2027.
  • October 2026: Managers may invest in IPOs, debt primary issues, listed securities, money market instruments, mutual funds; also foreign securities, unlisted securities, exchange-traded derivatives.

Traps

  • Discretionary managers execute portfolio adjustments on behalf of the client without prior trade confirmation.
  • Client accounts remain distinct individual segregated portfolios rather than collective pooled investment vehicles.

In the news

  • Oct 2026: Portfolio Managers Regulations, 2026 + PRIM route
  • Oct 2026: SEBI eases co-investment PMS norms for AIF managers

23/23★ Must-learnInternational Financial Services Centres Authority

In plain words

A unified statutory regulator governing financial institutions, financial products, and securities transactions within special international offshore financial zones.

Why it exists

  • Cross-border financial transactions conducted through domestic banking channels faced complex fragmented domestic regulatory overlapping.
  • A single offshore authority provides competitive global financial regulations to repatriate financial services onshore.

How it works

  • The authority exercises consolidated regulatory powers of domestic regulators over entities located within the designated international zone.
  • Global institutions establish offshore banking units, international exchanges, and insurance offices operating in freely convertible foreign currencies.
  • Cross-border asset trades and international debt listings take place under competitive tax and regulatory regimes.

Fixed facts

  • IFSCA IFSCA Act 2019; set up 2020; HQ GIFT City, Gandhinagar
  • IFSC-listed companies: MPS reduced from 25% to 10%
  • Permitted exchanges: India INX and NSE IX (both IFSC, GIFT City)

How it changed

  • May 2026: IFSC-listed companies: MPS reduced from 25% to 10%

Traps

  • Entities operating inside the financial centre are treated as non-resident offshore units under currency regulations.
  • Regulatory oversight is unified under the dedicated authority rather than dispersed across domestic agencies.

In the news

  • Nov 2026: SEBI permits depository receipts (DRs) for REITs and InvITs
  • May 2026: IFSCA: MPS for listed companies cut to 10%

Static Bank · Section 5Government Committees, Commissions and Reports13 items · 9 ★ must-learn · 4 ☆ good to know

Memory tricks

A committee or commission is set up to study one problem and make recommendations; it has no power to force the Government to accept them.

The Finance Commission is the exception: it is a constitutional body (Art 280) that decides how tax money is shared between Centre and States.

Banking, fiscal and tax committees led to many of the reforms in earlier sections; each row gives the year and the result.

5.1 Finance Commissions

1/13★ Must-learnFinance Commission basics

In plain words

The Finance Commission is the body set up every five years to decide how tax money is shared between the Centre and the States.

  • Art 280 → President constitutes it every 5 years | chairman + 4 members | conditions of service → Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1951
  • Art 281 → President lays its report before Parliament with an explanatory memorandum (action taken)
  • Recommends → vertical devolution (Centre → states share of net tax proceeds), horizontal devolution (among states), grants-in-aid (Art 275), local body grants, and disaster funding
  • Recommendations are advisory, but conventionally accepted
  • Art 270 → taxes shared between Centre and states | cess and surcharge stay outside the divisible pool
Memory tricks

280 = Constitutes, 281 = Reports to Parliament (28 + 0/1: "zero starts, one lays it before").

6/13★ Must-learnRBI Economic Capital Framework (Bimal Jalan, 2018-19)

In plain words

This committee looked at how much capital the RBI should keep as a cushion and how much of its surplus it can pass to the Government.

  • Committee set up by RBI in Nov 2018 under Bimal Jalan (former Governor) | accepted in Aug 2019
  • Two components of economic capital → realised equity (the Contingent Risk Buffer, CRB) and revaluation balances
  • CRB range → 5.5% to 6.5% of RBI's balance sheet | RBI set it at 5.5% in 2019 (was 6.5% as at 31 Mar 2024)
  • Framework to be reviewed every 5 years | an RBI internal committee is reviewing it (Governor Malhotra, Feb 2025)
  • RBI's accounting year July–June aligned with April–March from 2020-21; interim dividends only in extraordinary conditions

FY20 / FY21 / FY22 / FY23₹57,128 crore / ₹99,122 crore / ₹30,307 crore / ₹87,416 crore
FY24₹2.1 lakh crore (highest ever at the time)

12/13★ Must-learnPeriodic Labour Force Survey

In plain words

A nationwide statistical survey providing frequent estimates of labour market indicators including employment, unemployment, and participation rates.

Why it exists

  • Earlier quinquennial employment surveys failed to track rapid labour market shifts and emerging employment trends.
  • Frequent quarterly urban and annual rural surveys provide reliable timely data for evidence-based macroeconomic policymaking.

How it works

  • The national statistical office conducts probability sampling of rural and urban households across all administrative units.
  • Field enumerators record activity statuses, hours worked, earnings, and industry classifications using standardised questionnaires.
  • Data processing compiles participation rates, worker population ratios, and open unemployment rates.

Fixed facts

  • Periodic Labour Force Survey (NSO, MoSPI); usual status (ps+ss), age 15+
  • LFPR 59.3% (male 79.1%, female 40.0%) | WPR 57.4% | UR 3.1% (male 3.3% → 3.1%; female 3.1%)
  • Youth (15–29) UR 10.3% → 9.9%; rural youth 8.3%; urban youth 13.6%; urban UR 4.8%; rural UR 2.4%

How it changed

  • November 2026: Rural unemployment 4.2% (from 4.6%); rural female unemployment 3.9%, the lowest recorded in 2026; rural LFPR 58%; rural female LFPR 38.9%; urban female LFPR 25.9%.
  • September 2026: Unemployment rate, overall 5.1% (was 5.4% previous quarter)

Traps

  • Usual status measures activity over a longer reference year rather than current weekly status.
  • The survey measures both rural annual households and quarterly rotational urban samples.

In the news

  • Nov 2026: PLFS quarterly bulletin (July–September 2026)
  • Oct 2026: PLFS monthly bulletin, September 2026
  • Apr 2026: PLFS annual report 2024-25
  • Jan Mar 2026: PLFS quarterly bulletin (October–December 2025)

13/13★ Must-learnAnnual Survey of Industries framework

In plain words

The principal statistical survey capturing detailed economic parameters, capital structure, and employment in the registered manufacturing sector.

Why it exists

  • Macroeconomic national accounting requires reliable empirical data on industrial output, value addition, and factory employment.
  • A comprehensive census of registered industrial units provides foundational data for industrial policy formulation and economic planning.

How it works

  • Statistical authorities enumerate registered factories meeting threshold employment criteria across nationwide industrial zones.
  • Enterprises furnish audited records detailing fixed capital investments, fuel consumption, raw material inputs, and wages paid.
  • Aggregated survey outputs compute manufacturing gross value added, capital formation, and employment growth across industrial categories.

Fixed facts

  • Top 5 states by GVA (over 54%): Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh
  • Top 5 industries by employment (over 41%): food products, textiles, basic metals, motor vehicles, wearing apparel
  • Gross value of plant and machinery (registered manufacturing): up 7.25%

How it changed

  • November 2026: Top 5 states by GVA (over 54%): Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh
  • November 2026: Top 5 industries by employment (over 41%): food products, textiles, basic metals, motor vehicles, wearing apparel

Traps

  • The survey covers formal registered factories under the Factories Act rather than the unorganised informal manufacturing sector.
  • Gross value added reflects industrial output net of intermediate manufacturing consumption.

In the news

  • Nov 2026: ASI 2024-25 results
  • Oct 2026: ASI 2024-25

Static Bank · Section 6Schemes and Acts with Launch Year and Ministry22 items · 13 ★ must-learn · 9 ☆ good to know

Memory tricks

A scheme is a Government programme run by a ministry for a target group; the key facts are launch year, ministry and target group.

An Act is a law passed by Parliament; the Acts table lists the year and the ministry responsible.

Check the "Launch, Ministry, Target group" columns first; those are the most common questions.

6.1 Financial inclusion and social security

SchemeLaunchMinistryTarget groupKey feature

3/22★ Must-learnPM SVANidhi (restructured 2025)

In plain words

PM SVANidhi gives small working-capital loans to street vendors; this card gives its restructuring in 2025.

  • Full form → Pradhan Mantri Street Vendor's AtmaNirbhar Nidhi | Central sector scheme of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs | launched 2020 (Covid relief)
  • Cabinet approved restructuring on 27 Aug 2025 → lending period extended to 31 Mar 2030 (earlier ended 31 Dec 2024) | outlay ₹7,332 crore | target 1.15 crore vendors, including 50 lakh new
  • Loan ladder (enhanced): ₹15,000 (was ₹10,000, 12 months) → ₹25,000 (was ₹20,000, 18 months) → ₹50,000 (unchanged, 36 months)
  • Extras → 7% interest subvention on timely repayment | UPI-linked RuPay credit card after repaying the second loan | digital cashback up to ₹1,600 | coverage widened to census towns and peri-urban areas
Memory tricks

"15-25-50" replaces "10-20-50": only the first two tranches moved.

4/22☆ Good to knowSovereign Gold Bonds (SGB)

  • Launched 5 Nov 2015 alongside the Gold Monetisation Scheme and Indian Gold Coin; notified 14 Jan 2016 under the Government Securities Act 2006
  • Issued by RBI on behalf of the Government of India; denominated in grams (1 gram and multiples)
  • Interest 2.5% a year, paid half-yearly; tenor 8 years, premature exit after the 5th year, on interest dates
  • Eligible: resident individuals, HUFs, trusts, universities, charitable institutions; limit up to 4 kg per financial year
  • Capital gains on redemption exempt for individuals (from tax year 2026-27, only for bonds bought at original issue and held to maturity); interest taxed at slab rates
  • Last tranche: Series 2023-24 IV (21 Feb 2024); Government confirmed in Feb 2025 that no further tranches will be issued; existing bonds continue
Memory tricks

2.5 – 8 – 5 = interest %, years to maturity, year of exit.

6.2 Employment, labour and rural livelihoods

5/22★ Must-learnVB-G RAM G Act, 2025 (replaced MGNREGA)

In plain words

This Act replaced the MGNREGA rural job law with a new guaranteed-employment law.

  • Full form → Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 | Ministry of Rural Development
  • Bill introduced in Lok Sabha 16 Dec 2025 (Shivraj Singh Chouhan) → passed → President's assent Dec 2025
  • Repeals MGNREGA 2005 | in force from 1 Jul 2026 (MGNREGA provisions continued during the interim)
  • Guarantee raised 100 → 125 days of wage employment per rural household per financial year
  • Focus on durable infrastructure and digital governance; existing e-KYC job cards stay valid until new cards are issued

How it works → Rural household registers → demand for work → employment within the guarantee of 125 days → wages paid → assets created (infrastructure) → payment in lieu if work is not provided.

Memory tricks

"100 to 125", "2005 to 2025", "1 July 2026".

6/22★ Must-learnPM Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana (PM-VBRY)

In plain words

This scheme gives incentives linked to new jobs created, for both employers and first-time workers.

  • Earlier called ELI (Employment Linked Incentive) | Cabinet approval 1 Jul 2025 | effective 1 Aug 2025 | announced by PM on 15 Aug 2025 | Ministry of Labour and Employment, via EPFO
  • Outlay ₹99,446 crore | aim → 3.5 crore jobs (1.92 crore first-timers) | jobs created from 1 Aug 2025 to 31 Jul 2027
  • First-time employees (salary up to ₹1 lakh) → one month's EPF wage, up to ₹15,000, in two instalments after 6 and 12 months (second needs a financial literacy programme)
  • Employers → up to ₹3,000 a month per additional employee; extra bonus for manufacturing
Memory tricks

"99,446 crore, 3.5 crore jobs, 15,000 first pay".

7/22★ Must-learnFour Labour Codes (in force 21 Nov 2025)

In plain words

The four Labour Codes merge many older labour laws into four, covering wages, industrial relations, social security and workplace safety.

CodeLaws merged
Code on Wages, 20194 (Payment of Wages, Minimum Wages, Payment of Bonus, Equal Remuneration)
Industrial Relations Code, 20203 (Industrial Disputes, Trade Unions, Standing Orders)
Code on Social Security, 20209 (including EPF Act, ESI Act, Maternity Benefit, Gratuity)
OSH Code, 2020 (Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions)13 (including Factories Act, Mines Act)
  • 4 + 3 + 9 + 13 = 29 central labour laws replaced | Ministry of Labour and Employment | all four notified in force on 21 Nov 2025, some provisions to be phased in
  • Coverage extended to unorganised, gig and platform workers
Memory tricks

"4-3-9-13 = 29": Wages 4, IR 3, Social Security 9, OSH 13.

  • Sept 2026: Cabinet raised the mandatory-coverage wage ceiling ₹15,000 → ₹25,000 a month (₹15,000 since Sept 2014); about 51 lakh more employees covered; annual Government outgo about ₹11,339 crore; effective 17 Sep 2026

11/22☆ Good to knowOperation Flood and the White Revolution

  • Operation Flood launched 13 Jan 1970 by NDDB (National Dairy Development Board, Anand, Gujarat); architect Verghese Kurien, "Milkman of India"
  • Phases: I 1970–80, II 1981–85, III 1985–96
  • Funded by sale of skimmed milk powder and butter oil gifted by the EEC (European Economic Community) through the World Food Programme; Phase II also had a World Bank loan
  • Model: Amul (Kaira District Cooperative Milk Producers' Union, Anand; Tribhuvandas Patel) → a national milk grid
  • India became the world's largest milk producer in 1998, passing the US

19/22★ Must-learnBeti Bachao Beti Padhao (BBBP)

In plain words

Beti Bachao Beti Padhao is a campaign to improve the child sex ratio and to promote girls' education.

ItemKey facts
Launch22 Jan 2015
MinistryWomen and Child Development; Health (data) and Education are partners
AimRaise the child sex ratio; change mindsets about the girl child; girls\' education and empowerment
FundsAllocated to districts by sex-ratio-at-birth (SRB) status, using 2020-21 HMIS data
2021Merged into Mission Shakti (now a component of its SAMBAL vertical)
15th Finance Commission periodExtended to all districts; activities focused on behaviour change, so beneficiaries cannot be counted
SRB (HMIS)918 (2014-15) → 929 (2024-25)
Girls\' secondary GER (UDISE)75.51% (2014-15) → 83.4% (2025-26)
  • Related: PM Matru Vandana Yojana (since 1 Jan 2017; ₹5,000 for the first child via DBT, ₹6,000 for a second girl child); ₹20,446 crore paid to about 4.35 crore women up to 15 Jul 2026
  • Criticism: 54% of spending went to media and advocacy; only 18% of the ₹222 crore allocated for 2022-23 was used by Dec 2022; a July 2024 paper found no significant impact on enrolment; budget hard to track after the Mission Shakti merger
  • Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana was launched with it on the same date (see the savings-schemes card)
Exam angle

When was BBBP launched, and under which umbrella scheme does it now sit?

Memory tricks

B-B-B-P = 2015 → 2021 → 2024-25: launch (2015) → merged into Mission Shakti (2021) → SRB 929 (2024-25).

918 → 929: "9-1-8 to 9-2-9" (SRB rose by 11 points).

6/23★ Must-learnOPEC, OPEC+ and the UAE exit

In plain words

OPEC is a group of oil-producing countries that coordinate how much oil they produce; the UAE left it in 2026.

  • UAE exit → announced 28 Apr 2026; effective 1 May 2026 from OPEC and OPEC+ after a review of its production policy and capacity; the UAE had joined OPEC in 1967
  • OPEC (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) → founded at Baghdad in 1960; founders Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Venezuela; HQ Vienna; had 12 members including the UAE; publishes the World Oil Outlook
  • OPEC+ (Vienna Group, 2016) → OPEC plus 10 non-OPEC states: Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Brunei, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Mexico, Oman, Russia, South Sudan, Sudan
Exam angle

Which country left OPEC and OPEC+ on 1 May 2026?

Memory tricks

Founders = I-I-K-S-V (Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi, Venezuela). OPEC+ born 2016.

13/23☆ Good to knowRamsar Convention and India's wetland sites

  • Ramsar Convention: adopted 1971 at Ramsar, Iran; in force 1975; India joined 1982
  • India has 103 Ramsar sites across 28 States and UTs (as of 15 Oct 2026): latest additions Sukhna Wetland (Chandigarh) and Sauj Jheel (Uttar Pradesh); Glaw Lake became Arunachal Pradesh's first (3 Aug 2026)
  • Most sites: Tamil Nadu 20, then Uttar Pradesh 14; largest site: Sundarban Wetland (West Bengal), about 4,230 sq km
Remember

The count changes every few months; always check the latest figure in the monthly notes.

Ramsar 71 → 75 → 82: adopted, in force, India joins.

16/23★ Must-learnIndia's climate framework: NAPCC and NDCs

In plain words

India's climate plan has a national action plan and pledges (NDCs) made under the Paris Agreement; the table gives each.

ItemKey facts
NAPCC (National Action Plan on Climate Change)Launched 30 Jun 2008 under the Prime Minister's Council on Climate Change; MoEFCC coordinates; 8 original missions + Climate Change and Human Health (9 now): Solar; Enhanced Energy Efficiency; Sustainable Habitat; Water; Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem; Green India; Sustainable Agriculture; Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change
INDC / first NDC (2015)Emission intensity of GDP down 33–35% by 2030 (vs 2005); about 40% non-fossil power capacity by 2030; extra carbon sink 2.5–3 bn t CO₂e
Updated NDC (2022)Emission intensity −45% by 2030; LT-LEDS 2022 → net-zero 2070 (announced at COP26, 2021)
NDC 2031–35 (Cabinet approved; submitted to UNFCCC)Emission intensity −47% by 2035; 60% non-fossil installed capacity; carbon sink 3.5–4.0 bn t CO₂e; basis: first Global Stocktake and CBDR-RC (Common but Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities)
ProgressIntensity cut 36% (2005–2020); non-fossil share 52.57% (Feb 2026); 2030 targets of 33–35% intensity and 40% non-fossil already met
OtherLiFE; Ek Ped Maa Ke Nam; Green Hydrogen Mission (2023; 5 MMT by 2030); Net Zero Portal and NAPCC portal launched Sept 2026
Kigali AmendmentIndia ratified Sept 2021 (in force 26 Dec 2021); HFC phase-down from 2032: 10% → 20% (2037) → 30% (2042) → 85% (2047); World Ozone Day 16 Sep
Exam angle

What are India's NDC targets for 2035, and when was the NAPCC launched?

Memory tricks

Intensity cut: 35 (2015) → 45 (2022) → 47 (2035). Non-fossil capacity: 40 (2030, already met) → 60 (2035). Sink: 2.5–3 → 3.5–4 bn t. Net-zero 2070.

17/23☆ Good to knowCarbon markets and trade: CCTS, PACM, CBAM

  • CCTS (Carbon Credit Trading Scheme) notified 2023; GEI (Greenhouse Gas Emission Intensity) targets are legally binding per unit of product
  • First notification (Oct 2025) → 282 entities in aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali, pulp and paper; 13 Jan 2026 → 208 more (petroleum refineries, petrochemicals, textiles, secondary aluminium) → about 490 entities
  • Indian Carbon Market Portal launched Mar 2026 at Prakriti 2026 (BEE, Bureau of Energy Efficiency, conference); 9 notified methodologies
  • PACM (Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism, Article 6.4) → first credits issued (a clean-cooking project in Myanmar)
  • EU CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism) → carbon tax on steel, cement, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen imports; transitional phase from 2023; fully in force 1 Jan 2026
  • UK CBAM → recognises India's CCTS for carbon-tax relief (Sept 2026)
  • MISHTI (Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats and Tangible Incomes) → launched 5 Jun 2023; 540 sq km; 2023-28; funded about 70% from CAMPA plus MGNREGS
Exam angle

What is CBAM, and which sectors does it cover?

7.8 Geography, heritage and awards: static facts in the news

23/23☆ Good to knowStatic one-liners from June–July 2026

  • NCR: about 55,083 sq km; Delhi, 13 districts of Haryana, 8 of Uttar Pradesh, 2 of Rajasthan
  • Rakhigarhi: largest known Harappan town; others are Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Ganweriwala (Pakistan) and Dholavira (Gujarat)
  • Snow leopard (Panthera uncia): 12 range countries; Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List; State animal of Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh
  • Mekedatu: Cauvery balancing reservoir near Kanakapura, Ramanagara district, Karnataka
  • India–Nepal border 1,751 km; five Indian States; disputes: Kalapani–Limpiyadhura–Lipulekh (Uttarakhand) and Susta (Bihar)
  • Pacific Ocean: largest; Mariana Trench 11,034 m deepest; Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman
  • Narmada: also Reva; longest west-flowing river; rises near Amarkantak; empties into the Gulf of Khambhat; Sardar Sarovar, Indira Sagar, Omkareshwar, Maheshwar
  • Loktak Lake: Moirang, Manipur; largest freshwater lake in the North-East; phumdis and Keibul Lamjao; Ramsar 1990; Montreux Record 1993
  • Black Sea: Bosphorus to Sea of Marmara; Kerch Strait to Sea of Azov; six coastal countries (Bulgaria, Ukraine, Russia, Georgia, Romania, Türkiye)
  • Jnanpith Award: established 1961; ₹11 lakh, bronze Vagdevi; any Eighth Schedule language
  • Muga silk (Assam): GI tag in 2007
  • Tarapur units 1 and 2 (1969, Maharashtra): oldest operating commercial reactors in the world
  • Mettur Dam: Kaveri, Salem; Salal Dam: Chenab, Reasi (J&K); Mullaperiyar: Periyar, Idukki (Kerala–Tamil Nadu dispute)
  • Nehru Trophy Boat Race: second Saturday of August, Punnamada Lake, Alappuzha
  • Sariska Tiger Reserve is in the Aravallis of Rajasthan; Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam is India's largest tiger reserve (Andhra Pradesh)
  • Sahariya tribe: PVTG in Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Chhattisgarh; Kuno National Park in the Gwalior–Chambal region
  • Indian Navy: coastline about 11,098 km, EEZ about 2.4 million sq km, sea lanes carrying about 90% of trade by volume; MoD "Decade of Transformation" 2023–2032
  • UN International Year of the Woman Farmer: 2026
  • MECON granted Miniratna Category-I status
